en: There will be deceit in their words,
There will be guile in their eyes.
If they have the strength,
They will wish to attack you!
There will be crookedness in their words,
There will be a slant in their eyes.
If they find an opening,
They will wish to destroy you.
By asking, they will learn your whereabouts;
If you lie unprepared,
One day they will raid your village!
So that you do not submit to this,
Prepare coats no shot can pierce,
Prepare horses no shot can catch.
My Manas, touched by Kydyr,
All the mighty ones will meet you;
To you, touched by Kydyr,
All the valiant ones will come!
Fatten your horses and ready yourself;
Make your dear companions forty.
Do not be defeated to no purpose;
Choose your dear companions!
Now, Manas, hear my words!
The man who will listen to speech,
Subdue him with your speech.
The man who enters the faith,
Subdue him with your faith!
When you migrate farther from here,
At the lower end of Sary-Özön,
Renowned Talas, great Keng-Kol,
Make this land your dwelling;
Tend your Kyrgyz people.
Tend Talas and make it a fortress!
These are your elder lord Koshoy's words.
If you secure Talas,
It is a fortress against the world!
No unwary man has ridden over its passes,
No enemy facing it has prevailed.
No man has scouted its hollows,
No man has climbed upward there.
Make Talas your dwelling place.
We have raised as khan
Manas, son of Jakyp.
If we set our faces, we shall go to war;
We shall hear of his prowess.
My champion Manas, be safe!
I shall bind you as a brace to my back.
My support, Manas, with you here,
If strife and trouble rise from Beijing,
I shall pursue them to the Chinese empire.
Your dear elder, aged Koshoy,
Leopard Manas, you yourself,
I shall hold as my support.
You are my lord, my support;
Fortunate Manas, be safe!
A young gray hawk flown from the nest,
You are my surpassingly born lion.
Taking heart and drawing strength,
Your strong-backed land of Talas,
I shall make my refuge
A warrior like you, blessed by Kydyr.
Yesterday, when the Chinese oppressed us,
When they broke and slaughtered my band,
When they raised a tumult,
When they plundered my band,
Against the Chinese swarming over the land
I began a thorough rebellion.
I had no support to lean upon,
My champion, no warrior like you;
I let the great people be slaughtered,
And afterward I fled.
From lean I grew fat,
From hungry I became full,
From poverty I became rich,
From loneliness I grew numerous.
That dear land, Zheti-Özön,
By valor I made it my land;
The Kyrgyz of Zheti-Özön,
With difficulty I made them a people.
I may devote myself to Allah,
I may sacrifice myself to God:
Manas has been found in Altai,
And thus my honor is restored.
When your elder Koshoy dies,
You will dig his grave wide and hollow it,
You will slaughter his horse Kabylan;
Trampling with your own hand,
You yourself will bury your elder!”
His great eyes like Venus,
Ah, his ears like shields,
Your aged elder Koshoy
Now left off speaking.
Driven away without a way out,
His hands bound behind his back,
Grieving and sorrowing,
Unable to collect himself,
Parted from the Noygut people,
Akbaltay began to speak:
“King Manas, leopard!
When I dreamed a wondrous good dream,
You who came into the world,
By the might of Allah Most High,
My champion openly bestowed,
Grieving, being slaughtered,
The great people all raided together—
Of Jakyp and Baltay's forty households,
The people's lone warrior Manas,
Found for their good fortune,
My hawk, an ornament upon my forehead,
All grief has left my heart.
My son Manas, consider:
I am thinking of my people!
‘May they be safe,’ I pray,
Lion Manas, my darling!
When I go outside and look,
When I wish the people well,
We grieved, burning, scorched;
The many Chinese broke our band,
From all our people with their royal court
We were parted in devastation.
We tended Altai and made it our land;
The Black Kalmyks and Manchus,
Though unbelievers, we made our people.
When your age reached nine,
Leopard Manas, my foal,
We took you alone for our support.
Until your age reached ten,
Among Black Kalmyks and Manchus
We gave you the name Big Madcap.
When your age reached ten,
You began your terrible wrath;
Of the children who were playing,
You slaughtered eighty.
When you reached eleven,
You thinned the village headmen's ranks.
When you reached twelve,
You broke royal courts and took spoils;
Drinking blood, you grew hardened.
Among Black Kalmyks and Manchus,
You were named Bloodthirsty Manas.
When your age reached thirteen,
You broke royal courts and fired shots.
You grew hardened, sated with blood,
Among the seething Chinese,
You were named the Bloodthirsty Burut.
When you swayed in single combat,
No man came to match you.
You made all share in the excitement;
Fighting forty-two days,
By the teeming Chinese
You let your forty boys be slain.
Great Beijing, beyond the reach of floodwater,
The great surging army overran.
You turned your intent toward righteousness;
Of the Black Kalmyks and Manchus,
You shattered the countless troops
And freed your people.
You joined what was broken,
You gathered what was scattered.
My son Manas, from you yourself
I am asking for one thing.
I miss my land of Sary-Kol,
I often recall my Noygut people.
I earnestly beg, mighty Manas:
Let me attain my wish.
If you grant him as a worthy gift,
Let me take Kutubiy!
If I reach my people safely,
The foal of the fortunate lord,
Over my wretched Noygut people,
Let me raise him as khan!
‘My son is Manas's equal,’ I shall say,
And make him my refuge.
I have my hilly land of Sary-Kol,
I have my honorable Noygut people!
Among those Noygut people of ours,
There is more rice than common grain,
There is more silver than tin,
There are more foxes than gray hares,
Much wealth is heaped at their thresholds.
With jeweled braid ornaments and broad hips,
The Noygut people have beautiful brides;
In crimson dresses, with slender waists,
The Noygut people have beautiful girls.
Wild-sheep legs, bronze forelegs,
The Noyguts have swift horses;
In red dresses, with slender waists,
The Noyguts have beautiful girls.
Among our Noygut people,
With black hats like cauldrons,
Those are the Noygut warriors.
Unbelievers and Muslims
Are free to do as they wish.
There are more camels than cattle,
There are more giants than ordinary men,
There are many high, stony cliffs.
When I have passed away,
Against these Noygut people of mine
There are many enemies who will besiege them.
When the Chinese captured me,
When they cruelly put me in their net,
My settled people, the many Noyguts,
Were left abandoned, suffering orphanhood.
I have land left without people;
Wandering, unable to find their senses,
I have a people bereft of their senses.
If I gather my people and make them a people,
If I possess my land and make it my land,
If I gather the settled people,
To you, bloodthirsty leopard,
Shall I not stand as a wing!
Finding support in a known land,
Finding people who will be a firm support,
When I dwell among the vast Noyguts,
I have a name: Akbaltay.
In Sary-Kol, left in mourning,
I have abundant livestock, no children;
I have exactly sixty wives!”
Akbaltay spoke his various words,
Asked leave, and stopped.
Ill-intentioned Jakyp's
Heart burned and became a live coal!
“You mean to leave for your land,
Oh, Akbaltay, my soul's friend!
When my father Karakan died,
Karakan's countless riches,
The Black Kalmyks and many Manchus,
Divided them, measuring by their whips,
When they plundered the spoils,
When the Kalmyks raised havoc,
Karakan's eight sons,
All of us, single-born and twins,
When they cast us all into torment,
When they divided all of us,
No village remained camped on the terrace,
No news of where they had gone.
We went and turned toward Altai;
Through grievous, difficult affairs,
We were parted from our brothers.
Our heads were cast into distant lands;
Wandering and roaming, our strength departed.
Pressed by the Chinese army,
We were all slaughtered;
Parted from our people blessed by Kydyr,
Our lament reached God!
Your Chinese began the slaughter;
Sixty women, your widowed sisters-in-law,
My village was left desolate.
Driven out, we came to Altai,
Wandering, unable to find a way.
I remained as a support,
You were there as a father.
Having grown strong in Altai,
We migrated and returned here.
Your many people have come to mind;
My gray-maned Baltay, be safe!
